Good morning Luca,



Yesterday, news broke that the Turkish delivery operations of Getir, the delivery platform that was once the shining star of the country’s startup ecosystem, was sold to Uber for $335m.



The deal underlines the ups and downs Turkey’s startup ecosystem has had in recent years.



At the height of the pandemic funding boom in 2022, startups in the country raised more than $3.2bn, largely due to blockbuster raises from the likes of e-commerce site Trendyol and delivery startup Getir, which at its peak was valued close to $12bn.



However, since then less funding has gone to Turkish startups; last year they raised a mere $650m, according to Dealroom.



But that’s not to say there aren’t bright spots. Thanks to its highly digitised banking sector and large population, the country’s fintech scene is on the rise and home to several emerging startups.



It’s also flexed its muscles in gaming — Good Job Games, a mobile game development studio based in Istanbul, raised a $60m Series A last July from big-name investors such as Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures.

title: FW: 11/02/26: Scalable verliert an Dynamik, Live-Blog zur Commerzbank
content:
________________________________
From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de>
Sent: Wednesday, 11 February 2026 06:24:42 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna
To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com>
Subject: 11/02/26: Scalable verliert an Dynamik, Live-Blog zur Commerzbank

Außerdem: Wie's zum Karten-GAU bei der Coba kam (vor der Paywall)
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png]
Anzeige
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/504fd4cf-3171-5b9f-3630-855e5621b218.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=2e7e83343d&e=8f69674dd2>
Hebt die Commerzbank heute ihr Jahresziel an? Unser Live-Blog zu den Zahlen

Schön war natürlich nicht, was die Commerzbank in den letzten Wochen über sich lesen musste (siehe u.a. > Drama in zehn Akten  wie der Aquila-Kauf zum Fiasko geriet<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c976f6b282&e=8f69674dd2>). Wenn die Frankfurter allerdings heute ihre Bilanz-PK abhalten wird, dann soll das Debakel bei der Asset-Management-Tochter zur Fußnote schrumpfen. Schließlich lief das übrige Geschäft dermaßen rund, dass die Commerzbank gestern Mittag als kleinen Appetizer zu den heutigen Zahlen schon mal ihr Nettoergebnis von 2,63 Mrd. Euro in die Welt hinaus posaunen durfte<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0b755450b3&e=8f69674dd2> (nebst der ad-hoc-pflichtigen Ankündigung eines weiteren Aktienrückkaufs). Spannender wird derweil der Blick nach vorn  und zwar aus folgendem Grund: Laut ihrer Anfang letzten Jahres präsentierten Strategie rechnet die Commerzbank für 2026 offiziell mit einem Zinsüberschuss von 8,0 Mrd. Euro. Inoffiziell gilt diese Annahme aber längst als obsolet, immerhin kalkulieren die Analysten inzwischen im Schnitt mit 8,5 Mrd. Euro (das Delta von 500 Mio. Euro entspricht übrigens dem Zweieinhalbfachen dessen, was die Commerzbank vor zwei Jahren als Kaufpreis für Aquila Capital hingelegt hatte  so viel zu den Dimensionen). In den letzten Jahren hat der Vorstand in vergleichbaren Konstellationen meist nach dem Grundsatz "Underpromise & Overdeliver" agiert. Aber kann er sich eine derart defensive Gangart aktuell leisten, angesichts des wieder mal rekordhohen Aktienkurses und der extremen Vorgaben<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=41973d0506&e=8f69674dd2>, die zu Beginn der Woche von der Unicredit (also vom eigenen 30%-Gesellschafter) kamen? Es ist also ordentlich Pfeffer drin heute Früh. In unserem Live-Blog erhalten Sie bis 7.15 Uhr eine erste Kurzeinschätzung, bis spätestens 7.55 Uhr folgt eine erste Analyse. Bitte sehr: Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=50979f92ff&e=8f69674dd2>

Anzeige
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/262f5957-780c-c506-20bd-75b29aa05d23.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=9180afdf4a&e=8f69674dd2>
Mobile Investing boomt: Intuitive Apps, transparente Preise und smarte DIY-Tools gewinnen neue Generationen von Anlegern. Neobroker wachsen rasant  Banken müssen reagieren. Erfahren Sie in unserer aktuellen Studie, wie Mobile Investing das Retailbanking verändert, welche Erfolgsfaktoren über langfristige Relevanz entscheiden und was Banken jetzt tun sollten. Hier kostenlos herunterladen!<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=6784fc36d4&e=8f69674dd2>
Exklusiv: Wie es zum Karten-GAU bei der Commerzbank kam (frei zugänglich)

Wie kann es sein, dass Kriminelle von Brasilien aus mit gefälschten Girocards die Konten stinknormaler Commerzbank-Kunden plündern? Und wie kann es sein, dass der ganze Spuk erst gestoppt wird, als bereits ein Schaden in signifikant zweistelliger Millionenhöhe aufgelaufen ist? Genau diese Fragen umtrieben vor zwei Jahren die Payment-Aficionados dieser Republik. Eine verlässliche Erklärung allerdings hatte niemand. Vieles blieb These, vieles Spekulation. Was immerhin rasch klar war (und der unvergessene Jörg Oliveri del Castillo-Schulz hat's dann ja auch unverblümt betätigt): Die Sicherheitslücke, durch die die Cyber-Kriminellen geschlüpft waren, hatte sich nicht bei der Commerzbank selbst aufgetan  sondern bei ihrem Processing-Dienstleister, dem Kölner Bank-Verlag. Und der wiederum gab vor wenigen Wochen, also zwei Jahre nach dem "Karten-GAU", einen Einblick, was genau damals eigentlich schiefgelaufen ist. Unsere Recherche aus dem Januar, jetzt für kurze Zeit vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (10 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=6ec9729b92&e=8f69674dd2>

Briefing

Abflüsse aus offenen Immobilienfonds  Run auf ETFs hält an: Als die Deka dieser Tage zu Protokoll gab, im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr einen Nettozufluss in ihre offenen Immobilienfonds verbucht zu haben  da war das fast so etwas wie ein Hoffnungsschimmer für die kriselnde Branche. Zwar belief sich der Saldo zwischen Zu- und Abflüssen auf gerade mal 90 Mio. Euro. Aber immerhin kein Minus! Die gestern vorgestellten BVI-Zahlen freilich zeigen, dass die Deka damit die Ausnahme sein dürfte. Branchenweit flossen aus offenen Immobilienfonds allein im vierten Quartal weitere 2,0 Mrd. Euro an  die Jahresabflüsse addieren sich damit auf 7,7 Mrd. Euro (nach bereits 5,7 Mrd. Euro in 2024). Für betroffene Anbieter wie die Union Investment dürfte es immerhin ein Trost sein, dass Publikumsfonds insgesamt  also über alle Fondsgattungen hinweg  einen Nettozufluss von stolzen 86 Mrd. Euro verbuchten. Wobei: Zwei Drittel hiervon entfielen auf ETFs, also auf aus Anbietersicht tendenziell margenschwache Produkte.

title: Commerzbank CEO Orlopp Lifts Profit Guidance
content: Commerzbank CEO Bettina Orlopp speaks to Bloomberg as the lender lifted its guidance for profit this year after reporting higher-than-expected earnings in the fourth quarter. The results are a boost to Orlopp as she continues to defend the bank against a potential takeover from Italian rival UniCredit. She also discusses deregulation and the outlook for interest rates. Commerzbank gibt Widerstand auf  und macht nun doch bei Wero mit

Die Commerzbank vollzieht die Kehrtwende und schließt sich nun doch dem neuen Online-Bezahlverfahren Wero an. Der Vorstand habe kürzlich einen entsprechenden Grundsatzbeschluss gefasst, erklärte Vorstandschefin Bettina Orlopp am Vormittag bei der Bilanz-PK. Wie und wann Wero den eigenen Kunden angeboten werden soll, werde intern noch diskutiert. Für die hinter Wero stehende European Payments Initiative um EPI-Chefin Martina Weimert ist die Entscheidung ein eminent wichtiges Signal. Die Commerzbank hatte ursprünglich zu den Protagonisten der pan-europäischen Bezahlinitiative gehört, sich nach dem Scheitern der ursprünglichen EPI-Pläne allerdings Anfang 2022 entnervt zurückgezogen. Dass die Frankfurter nun doch wieder mitmachen (wenn auch mutmaßlich erst einmal nur als Nutzer, nicht als Shareholder) könnte darauf hindeuten, dass es unter Kunden mittlerweile tatsächlich eine gesteigerte Nachfrage nach Wero gibt.

Verkäuferinnen und Verkäufer im Hawaiihemd, Schatzsuche für Groß und Klein, so geht Einkaufen bei Trader Joes. Dazu gehören die ständig neuen Artikel mit fantasievollen Namen, die in antiquierten Schriftzügen auf der Verpackung prangen und auf scheinbar handgeschriebenen Tafeln angepriesen werden. Was das karibikbunte Ambiente in den Läden nicht unbedingt vermuten lässt: Die US-Supermarktkette ist im Besitz von Aldi.

Über Trader Joes spielt Aldi Nord in den USA mit. Die Übernahme der kalifornischen Hippiemarke durch Theo Albrecht im Jahr 1979 dürfte einer der besten Deals der Supermarktgeschichte gewesen sein. Aus den damals 20 Filialen sind heute 622 geworden. Hinter der sorgsam gepflegten Hippieromantik steckt knallhartes Wirtschaftskalkül in Aldi-Manier. Mit rund 70.000 Angestellten schafft Trader Joes die typisch lockere Einkaufsstimmung inklusive Small Talk an der Kasse. Das sind US-weit knapp 20.000 Leute mehr als bei Aldi Süd, die dort ein etwa viermal größeres Filialnetz betreiben. Aber es rechnet sich.   *   Es war überfällig, dass sich immer mehr Frauen selbst um ihr Geld und ihre finanzielle Absicherung kümmern. Viel zu lange haben viele das hintangestellt und Finanzfragen in Partnerschaften ihren Männern überlassen. Viel zu häufig ist Altersarmut auch heute noch weiblich. Doch seit Frauen stärker ihr persönliches Finanzmanagement übernehmen, ist auch der Markt für Finanzprodukte speziell für Frauen enorm gewachsen. Bei Weitem nicht alle Angebote sind seriös. Verbraucherschützer mahnen zur Vorsicht, vor allem bei Finanzwerbung über Social Media. AI eats the world

Okay so I have a business plan for Sam Altman. Heres what you do. You build an artificial intelligence application for some specific sort of business, coding<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Nm2f0N2YHTKuB661nibyOv46sHmTw9AE6HMsW9q0HtZr_2S1xFxGue1Jn1GnylAN6QWa3ozaeiRf8AN9PsGnWi8UazSvicNC6iKqnvLSQehsejlVMbB5O7jPkJJCZRRR1n5yJlr0FJR6ZK2BYmo7z0DCHu09GEcMDcltb8GO_-WoF7vy2rLNhKOifCvxha4hefu14xpxCdMXHRHke04_r77PpLugKnC5ff3UJ3g6IjhkDbBdgAl5H5qoOx3qnPrf0WXMlHrJeuhOT0NGMnc-Cdk2HMqoNnZm7FZs0I9_GDfiODv3TL63m6_zHy04VwP6WzsQeaoktMhZClGpZTAdV6jtgA3kTeP8F5cvKkz-npiFg6o8-QrHOf2siQ/gXdctU-5plPb0WVq6lptdM3TSJiDnDCj/17> or tax planning<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/HQVQxSGndkKLFsKYKrA7b92xDXlqWh6vdfGLg-3oQBjT-tRfIBG3dwdngm0XRRFpcnnx641TCH4Um-gZeSE_jqn7rZwCjFJZacuDL-pYBt16_s5AqTebJKv-pMtaI3VgE6e9UOMs0g2zAM0OjKh9uY2Dmb51WO5BY0spg6JL1d0cy7v6V6P2m8YpinbjM_4uy1_BKGdkjTwqenH6FhhCha4vYyC90vu-OJr7kUpK5OIPDy9RSycYgf3_7H9KlL_fY4x1JlfaBhcjwV7TKtEQo3dQ7rVYy1ik3PanZsAJRGOCD75D6akigoSTtWE6UNC8mYgJA1hdChf7dvbMS-MOuis3NVRlSsuJbzk9JDKO8lD0RExTQGckXHzVOQ/-cfMHXOASnVS86pBLxoAqi0VQVHQIeNe/17> or whatever. You roll it out on a Tuesday morning. You announce it in blandly optimistic terms and do some cool demos. You go on financial television, and when they ask you  as they will  a question like wont this disrupt the business model of software-as-a-service companies or wont this put financial advisers out of business, you smirk ruefully and shake your head and say well there is a lot of disruption coming, and it may be difficult to know<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/FQH8_o7JlKnEvAnIKghTgAq6tcOqdP4PvSjDPt140AdoRvl2Ap0hymSeXA0Z7kTdUnQjkPn8L4gJ95mI5zSYCdd9LrO5MchrzekP0mO9MJOG5J28c3rXhuWzxazzVwn3acUtWgCNuTzMR7SqdJTutY7yO1x7o3_TvO2f_ZYib_CHR2DfyB3SoI2oYGWKHQpEdNMcJynF4GfSdoeEAh9BXAUi_Q_bUTE9lxuSExcaU719tO3HJZ4o1BHjhVbF11CyvlB4VHo8e8BRaxiVTDBXcPb4gU9P_NUrvzmFWM2slbfblEbG2b95w3JgIIg3UYCWxanKQRAaKxOW_yC-lEO-76ksawMzW0tgniGaHuktRrj-XWO8bOBixDs2Eg/t_q3jluNOMZ9u3LCGvJf5fQjdY6fbd35/17> what role money will play in a post-artificial general intelligence world.

And by Tuesday afternoon every software company or wealth management company or whatever sector youre targeting will have sold off by like 10%. Oh and of course the other thing you do is, on Monday  before you announce the new product  you buy a bunch of put options on all of the software/wealth management/whatever companies stocks. And you make like a 1,000% one-day return on your money, probably not in huge size but in useful size.

And then you do it again next week. You have, let us hypothesize, built something that is artificial, pretty intelligent and pretty general. You have a quite smart robot. Robot, disrupt the X industry, you tell it each week for some new X. And each week you eat some industrys lunch and turn it into trading profits for yourself. Not investing advice!

Actually we have talked about this business model a few times before. I proposed it for OpenAI last year<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/VdrcdPZGVcX16z2TKrz2BF8SZ1H4lewDWNYPwuHM8qpxguxhwcM1r9x3vqLGCHI-SsFcQ2peq6mTE38aEBy-i6IhAagtdZvsoWDuQbikUPSx0s4dKSMqbuLtZYOQ_kjLD24nFYLaum8FSwX4kEQuQh-v_5S3QuVYvxWh-8-nOxRHEBq4LLzu-Nu4hFFQVJB580PtVL5punOhQQMelWdSYXzK0rkFI2D6LXHsrLanfFK3K3s4TmhIilRUtk1Io7No7Xa7Q_CXCPTN0Qab7qdP8VmF3j_fhUX1F-8K40l7LNROi8rw7VFaUcKnf1G8KA4506ARxGVfp_PeBJSr8Wm2b_ZPrqPY9PtHBOpK8uKjnoHTMydcmVfn3PFrDw/FzUdlK7gzbL6K9JnbAMtpE-m7uVinobp/17>, for instance, and I also wrote about it<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/IcKxrk0gPeVuTwp1uVOu88fs7B-tcLOHDCs0XtoL7kaskRSmbT6xm4s3h4oV9HyqcLTZujZ-8tuY4GDwNhvCTZUvpwHsPi1zQgrpvLWTfBHYm1v5kwwQFEV-G8ryIgwLhadsAbCeNBEp9R2Hq_3pPwbkyN1EuozQkSQIcJsOJP3ZfM8KxU52WSwCAiLbabFTP2SElRqBsCSbWdv2uY98-YaYH32eWyh2e_WYMBjPnGGNdyc4Egx7UybxNaapsre9_PVAievriiYtegYNojkn8hek5p4TlRduprpR8fzbNbKxy_FmlFeRKYJZ9W6A_logbyItb7FFJIA-jWwN-UV8NAI-bztTxLLJJ6s0tQQzDEABfYDPRFdloLkPBw/g7ihexuEezKA8qht7cSJmbXL1d3poXRm/17> when DeepSeek came out with a model that briefly crashed all the other AI stocks. And weve talked about the idea<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-Z7puxRrARUNK8NeWukfibUig6yb3OOyfLVmkDbOB7dxQlheWSO4X2MrPQnAj9XPTzCvMBJUJWHSaQYIgFuQRyNfVMJTwqhHhwxjtIoDq6VDyKcrPdily5q7dLZXZnXQa3QGvY_-QlJSm_9tPe1W8Pb9jNkqmBC9VTqP4x2A1rEbIAXWeXeT7wfr25CFx44F5Xk277jkNKPkHZ4cgjSXxxdmRS2sSCVDFqnWDdtxFO-B8hq_AQYWo7HQFSBGD618lytEwBAuixHb0W1dKMu16bqU24152wm2HcCvUCUA6M1LIx0hyyyhRN20wMjJWEa9713K7AFJAewnmjeqDqg13DtuSyozgbYQeGXfunffMkmUqjNy5sbWJywvSr4/kXSTXPscrHV2eWKoY1-qu5opYOOL43Fy/17>  short an incumbent industry, and then disrupt it  in other contexts; Joe Weisenthal proposed it decades ago<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/67JIFCoTLUkbCdQ24oKND0NFdbCa3GNjV5fmA78IPlicRHPwzr-sDt3axVnYvxx6La-K72gNeUzl-JX-HVUb7MQqn5-ONRCehv0eTer2q5Yalea9FtP1OFbjyh8gf3MW6kSA4OOBYJjovZ4vixfv9IJL5D6UEdOJkjZAsDh_0c2KijbZBu9G8gT5lqi0ILFD6NN8RLB8iQkqT6Q0Ud7ikz9wL3PO0xk07FD_6iiiSaqz7MUJoU3tSrCPxPump-Wab0qeGyNo0PjM5MGI920_IXTZmXfEpFZkvCxRCaOMkrDD0nw_FNHMl6gVyqIDEK5aZuHCctdPJ0eskxjCnFfV_LbJyijW1oAZGbzYS2F4p4GAtu1Sy1icf_F8WHo/oo7Rv0wMQNCOKoNB8XEYBorg2_kEQEpz/17>.

Of course it is not specific to Sam Altman. OpenAI is a big AI lab, and I sort of like the idea of him smirking through this short thesis on TV, but any AI lab could do it, or they could take turns. Or, more generally, every AI lab could short every industry, and then they could disrupt each industry when they get around to it.

I feel like one way to express the model is:

  1.  Right now, there is an economy. People spend trillions of dollars on goods and services, and many of those trillions of dollars go to big public companies as revenue.
  2.  In N years, AI will satisfy all human needs and desires, so people will not spend any more money on goods or services, and all of those companies revenues will go to zero. As I once put it<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/OCuGr9EZzB8sWxjG7Jyz-a8tMLKhxhSu2FWwfk88q5pSpqmnzCAz1_fBuG8Pl6RMKsATURT4Cmsc4XcYbqpq29Xa5V6dvV1Af2OLUZ2VBkvrhK429pEvjl6RVevwVWCLg0U40gJfFrE7F09y35IMylOyDkWkYmpHv_TqohLVbZf9wmkRfgT93cvpvac50qciArJYd8KDYFxqlL8OSgUDPOEa8dp43Nelg1tXYYlJLR3lUt2CTY6dO3NgREvyBub4l1CWWxpB7OcLvgcgU80gUuokqZsCdEwg3tsErY1qh_g13MSZIff6rhkuBLhUeYnksnKwH1Cr9X7lkVJZ3LUExapzaqxMxaKJZGRdFG1ne8rK34ep7zir1yBhPvc/Syc0G3N2HjzlONWrJoLFElUSYiX4L52C/17>, in talking about DeepSeek: Everyone has a magic lamp in their pocket with a genie that can grant unlimited wishes; the lamp is cheap and each wish is free.
  3.  One possibility is that, if you control the robots, then in N years all of those trillions of dollars of revenue that other companies currently get will go to you instead.
  4.  But this is not the only possibility. Maybe robot control will be competitive, the genie will be nearly free, and all of the revenue will just vanish, just become consumer surplus. (Or perhaps all of the profits will end up with the chip makers, or the electric utilities, or something, but not the AI labs<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/B1MseUARcQ-_bjupMPjuZGGDF26TglS3m15iJrmenTGy2cwFFRRX0XFr2UhbIGsKWs6SvU1G2N36wWv9Z2qgy0OLOlOhQ46n_w2MPMdYoOwOThSBhpqXvmuwfkwzfZ6-yGQeW1vNisbWeihiJ7bMPYGV92_6zV6mSh6bBtQ-4gGkYXJ-tV3Fjzi4NAmjoB1f1qVaacSPg_G_3Xl3lqV-ITU_mYeUZj2gAzz9dNj5mq6gS7Jv3oWlAyAzvP3k0s08EM5wbsHN__ADmWeYG66hcdJwENA_31WdBCJZD5CIrbN8sZEl60gUIUoVGNm39fJ-a7JzQ2_vuwo8PgbbOD1RNicGjJ_KHMCBxXX2mv9zqXFT5PORY4WrKrj4wSc/ypmALH0MytPK839vnK3OD3tVkQBXbUz_/17>.)
  5.  Or maybe the robot-controller will get rich, but it wont be OpenAI (or whichever other lab). If you are building the robots, you want to hedge your risk of losing to better robots in a winner-take-all competition.
  6.  Also you dont know what N is, and it might be a long time, and you need billions of dollars now to build more robots.
  7.  Also maybe this is all stupid. Everyone has a magic lamp in their pocket with a genie that can grant unlimited wishes, come on. You might want to hedge your risk that this is all wrong, that the revenue wont vanish, that the industries wont be disrupted, etc.

If the market now is both optimistic about AI and jumpy about its disruptive effect on other industries, you can monetize that jumpiness. If the market thinks that AI disruption will be this total, that AI will eat software and wealth management and everything else  or if the market just ascribes a meaningful probability to that  then you might as well capture that now.

The magic of financial markets<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/RJI0SSMbqk0yb7M_OOpAuE6kp1y9t_lOsT0I48ONrveTPKv9L-1i6R-PBdI2070uPbQ2t012sCCzCOexApPXhCE3NTUL6b64Xqp_A9DYSp0rFZQp4yWqf4VrVjpvFkQXsxTEZc0Ml8NARj807dTZUWNiz1MtLtKCqpmoDlfqNFQF501PbFvH_f6mcfwge7ldMVR598DmBcWrcNoQiu4YhYMeunFoslgix45lEu9j2VWxSZU-q6ftbaB_nTnN474lGW-tsnXpdoPvqd4lqGX31M3w1jAmRxmeT1AyeadE2VztiNZYNoe7O9x-w3jLKj6PnLpAu59hfkzOi9MzJZmEkHbTiu2sdUIOQjDM6t8QCOhWH0oNZYJ_MTnoTro/XFCPTlrcgnUiK7guiHMgeTqc2GOj7C3A/17> is that they can turn a bad future fact about the world like the revenue of Industry X will go down by $1 trillion into a positive amount of money, for you, now. (A negative amount for someone else, sure, but thats not your problem.) Also they can turn some probability of a bad future fact, or even some widespread beliefs about the probability of a bad future fact, into money for you now. Anyway<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/XUiCRrY5lnwIoFI7USpDo5efyqFx3yZwlty-BRy5iAUTyHyDwPtL6iMVYnjCn0HUmU2X6_MVrigcHg65-FME1oNSzsmHoVQ7UHD2nlCe4t4SXcqngZg6O0Vuza6ZHxoo427hQiJNAG68WPgYE_wzk-0A6nGAOMMubgkYxNgPYX7A5-gEjbde5Nv3Czjd-jBjUuvaW2rGbtsYJa4SOvynNRvAkNkYSh71B8Ab_4fYxklVx867pG0OUJwt-UH8Z2Bg0ly43YZhFB8ENU-gJrobhjsqfsCUHpm3WJO5yty4XiYKXXg6eCEPO_ZqAg5ganFCUlFVpZ6wplmEQZiS9-pt6K27YzgMAIdRINOjXvH3pQwxQHK8I4OR_d3TPdY/SaPixJD3EbyA0sP78G8i4OZKKLe3yvH_/17>:

On Wall Street, rising fears about artificial intelligence keep pummeling shares of companies at risk of being caught on the wrong side of it all, from small software makers to big wealth-management firms.

The latest selloff was triggered by a tax-strategy tool rolled out by a little-known startup, Altruist Corp. The perceived threat the sent shares of Charles Schwab Corp., Raymond James Financial Inc. and LPL Financial Holdings Inc. down by 7% or more, before going on to hit European companies, too.

It was the deepest slide for some of those stocks since the markets trade-war meltdown in April. But it was only the most recent example of a sell-first, ask-questions-later mentality that has rapidly taken hold as new products emerge from the hundreds of billions of dollars poured into AI, sowing anxiety about how the technology may upend entire industries.

Every company with any sort of potential disruption risk is getting sold indiscriminately, said John Belton, a money manager at Gabelli Funds.

If AI is destroying the current economy to build something new, maybe make some money on the destruction first.

Defeasance!

Companies often borrow money by issuing bonds. This gets them money, but it limits their flexibility. For one thing, they have to pay back the bonds: They have to make scheduled interest payments and pay back the principal at maturity, or else they will be in default and the bondholders will be able to sue to get all their money back. But thats not all. Bonds might also have covenants saying that the company cant do certain transactions  new borrowing, dividends, stock buybacks, etc.  and will often have change-of-control provisions saying that, if the company is acquired, it has to pay back its bonds immediately at 100 or, often, 101 cents on the dollar. The bondholders dont want the company to do risky things  borrowing more, getting bought in a leveraged buyout, etc.  that would endanger their payments, so they negotiate covenants to prevent that.

Sometimes a companys circumstances will change, and it will no longer want those limits on its flexibility. How can it get rid of them? Well, it could get rid of the bonds. How can it do that? Most corporate bonds are not freely callable; the company cant just give bondholders their money back anytime it wants. It can call up each bondholder and say hey wed like to buy back your bonds and negotiate a price, but thats administratively annoying and probably wont get everyone. It can do a tender offer, a public offer to buy back all of the bonds at the same price, but that probably wont get everyone either. (In particular, if bondholders know that the company needs to get rid of the bonds, they might hold out for a higher price.)

There is another, weirder way, at least sometimes. This is defeasance. Some bonds will have a provision saying that the company is allowed to defease them. To defease a bond, a company deposits all of the future interest and principal payments on the bond with the bonds trustee, and then it washes its hands of the bond. Roughly speaking, the bond is no longer the companys problem: The trustee has all the money it needs to make all the payments, so the company is off the hook. All those covenants  about not borrowing more money or doing mergers  no longer apply, because the bondholders no longer need to worry about the companys credit, because the money is already there.

There is one important simplification in the previous paragraph: I said that the company deposits all of the future interest and principal payments with the trustee, but it normally doesnt do that in cash. It normally does it in US Treasury securities. Consider, just hypothetically, a company that a few years ago issued a $750 million 30-year bond<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Zs-EOOG0S_470sc6z7vu4Z0CHRQBYCZb0n4XPHQcgGTZySuvv5HPJXk0NRq_3M4E_C-zotVUCp1ArH1pIG_rcJYMDwQNZezuKxzS-Ss3ULu-ppuIpHjRJRy81edz2ngbpnJfrIyjCEu4Y-Kc6KV_KbzKJDjfF0xi-TxunKyd7JYKZfe9SzfDb8enNx-9VR_znz4pkJxcjXa3-RQ4s7Skc85q8T_BYQ_Dq8mSKSHxIAr-9_kkv7Cf-oQftl8HBTTQs2tWCmtxw0kfO8A5boxhZ8DUpwZmiXLrCLJKceQ0LZi3aa6T1TtrsoadRQ7uguZFAlZz0-oQnsHzgtegQ1AXcFQiknEE5I9fisMIbBcA8IFiqBC7C1QFWsq6FbQ/9ER9HuHMtKmL-O2EIGeZqLbE5y5m_IeT/17> that matures in February 2051 and pays 2.95% annual interest. The company has to pay about $22.1 million of interest every year for the next 25 years (2.95% of $750 million), and then $750 million at maturity in 2051. If it decided to defease that bond, it could deposit $1.3 billion in cash ($750 million plus 25 years of $22.1 million interest payments) with the trustee, and then the trustee would have enough cash to pay off the bond.

But that would be dumb. Theres a US Treasury bond that matures around the same time and has a coupon of 3%. [1]  Theres about $54 billion of it outstanding. The company could just buy $750 million principal amount of that Treasury bond and deliver it to the trustee. Every year that Treasury bond would pay $22.5 million of interest, enough to cover the companys bonds interest payments, and in 2051 it would mature and pay $750 million, enough to cover the companys bonds principal. Perfect, done. Youve replaced the companys credit with US government credit, which seems like strictly an improvement. The bond is defeased, the bondholders are happy, and the company can walk away from the bond and its annoying covenants.

The nice thing about this trade, for the company, is that that Treasury bond is trading at about 74.5 cents on the dollar. The company could go out and buy $750 million principal amount of that bond for about $560 million. The company could completely satisfy its obligations under its own $750 million bond  a total of $1.3 billion of principal and interest  for a cash outlay of $560 million now.

Thats, you know, whatever, the magic of compound interest; the present value of those $1.3 billion of payments, discounted at the Treasury rate, is just $560 million. More specifically what is going on here is that both the company and the US Treasury issued 30-year bonds a few years ago, when long-term interest rates were very low, but now it is 2026 and long-term interest rates are higher. Back in 2021, a promise to pay $22 million a year for 30 years and then $750 million at the end was worth $750 million; now it is worth $560 million. [2]  Thats also the magic of interest rates.

Now forget about defeasance for the next two paragraphs. Say you bought that 30-year corporate bond back in 2021. You paid 100 cents on the dollar. Now interest rates are higher, and the bond is worth less. I said above 74.5 cents on the dollar, but thats for a Treasury bond with no credit risk; a corporate bond with credit risk might be worth 65 cents on the dollar. Getting paid 2.95% interest for the next 25 years is no longer that attractive a proposition, so you have lost money. Oh well.

But you still have those covenants, and every so often they generate a windfall. For instance: What if the company has a change of control? What if theres a leveraged buyout? Well, then it has to pay back its bonds at 101 cents on the dollar, right? Instead of paying you 100 cents on the dollar in 2051, which is worth about 65 cents today, the company would have to pay you 101 cents on the dollar right now, which is worth about 101 cents. Thats a big improvement!

Or it is, if you forgot about defeasance. But if the company can defease the bonds before its leveraged buyout, the covenants go away, and so does the change-of-control put at 101. Instead of getting 101 cents on the dollar today, you get exactly the contracted cash flows for the next 25 years, which are worth about 75 cents. [3] Oh well.

Bitcoin margin loan securitization

In the long run, loans want to be securitized. When some new form of lending is invented  art loans or crypto loans or whatever  the company that invents it will probably both (1) make the loans and (2) own the loans. The company will have some money, and it will meet with potential borrowers and evaluate them, and if it decides to lend them money, it will lend them its own money. That just feels right. The lender knows the borrowers, it has decided to trust them, it understands this new form of lending that it just invented. People who didnt invent this form of lending, who havent met with the borrowers, have no particular reason to give them money. The company making the decision is the company taking the risk. It has skin in the game.

But then the company will do this for a while and it will work pretty well and the company will make money and the new form of lending will take off, and eventually the company will realize that it has a lot of demand for loans and only so much money. So it will go to other people, outside investors, and say hey we are making all these loans and theyre going great and earning a high return, do you want some? And the outside investors will look at the companys track record and say something like hey you are earning high returns with low volatility and low correlation to other assets. They will say this in part because its true  a newly invented form of lending should have high returns (no one else does it) and low correlations (its not like everything else)  and in part because there is limited data: A newly invented form of lending hasnt been around for long enough for all of its risks to be realized.

But once it has been around for long enough to have some track record of good results, outside investors will be interested in getting in. So the company that makes the loans will be able to sell them to outside investors, who will not meet the borrowers and make the lending decisions themselves, but will trust some combination of (1) the pitch and documents and handshake that they get from the company that makes the loans and (2) the track record of the asset class. And ultimately there will be a division of labor between people who make the loans (who meet the customers and do the underwriting) and the people who own the loans (who put up the money). And this has various well-known problems, because the people making the loans have less skin in the game than they used to, though you can arrange the incentives to manage those problems.

This is all a sort of handwavy generic analysis and obviously not every sort of loan will be securitized, because not every category of loan will be big and popular and homogenous enough to be securitized. It is tempting to say something like a private banker or auction house might lend you some money against your art collection, but that is a bespoke deal with one-of-a-kind collateral and would be hard to securitize to outside investors. But in fact, sure, art loans get securitized<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/07PotUA3bxJmQBOneeXpYU98vj1Ud_SDkdiuHpYkIujae9AKKwtihLqf9z-XQSOs9cBjs0BiGpIBtbT9TOdJsGC7sN7oKdCPXiKvbVGKFe39tqgHOFbjEuTYfRM2D6Ek3fSYezQJ_eoHfs4OsDsE097z2C5pLk0Q3wKcOS4UF1W77RkfmuvhhrAuHNEw4wDl-A_zCaIHqOnCMX305Hk1Pl1YzWtQj9RLtoTPucX_q2SjYLgPZmOwV5SnR-5Ey67RdCJ2Ia7VFlwyXBEOy9O9Y-UZthnbxZYKi_NJsLsH31wlq8zkZiWMPic5fxoQJnV8lz-9eok21g05mIJY3cOqlvY16XEtxV-MklK11gvgHd4lvdiIdF5EBvuqcHk/cBR-CvOjLHovmPUhUbYfrueRUcOp8f7j/17>.
